11:47pm

Hey, so I just got out of the shower and there's another clump of hair in the drain. It's been happening for like two weeks now and I'm really freaking out. I'm on minocycline for acne, from Dr. Gallagher at student health, and I found "alopecia" in the tiny print on the leaflet. Does that mean I'm going bald permanently? Or is this some temporary thing? I feel like she should have warned me.

Two weeks of shedding is genuinely unsettling to notice, especially when you connect it to a medication leaflet — that's a reasonable thing to worry about, and you did the right thing by looking into it rather than ignoring it.

Here's the honest picture:

**What the leaflet means.** "Alopecia" on a drug leaflet means hair loss was reported in some patients taking the drug — it's listed because it happened, not because it's common or permanent. For minocycline specifically, hair loss is a rare reported side effect, and when it occurs it's typically **telogen effluvium** — a temporary shedding where hair follicles prematurely enter a resting phase and then regrow. That pattern doesn't cause permanent balding. It also usually shows up weeks after a trigger, not immediately, so two weeks of shedding could plausibly relate to the medication or to something else entirely.

**Other common causes worth knowing about.** Telogen effluvium is very common in college students and is often triggered by stress, illness (even a bad cold or COVID a couple months ago), significant weight loss or diet changes, iron deficiency, or thyroid issues. So minocycline is a candidate, but not the only one — and it may not be the cause at all.

**What actually matters for your hair's future:** in the vast majority of drug-induced or stress-induced shedding, hair regrows once the trigger is removed or resolves. This is not the same as male- or female-pattern baldness.

**What to do:**

1. **Contact Dr. Gallagher's office this week** — don't wait. Tell them the timeline and that you found alopecia listed. They may switch you to a different acne medication (there are good alternatives like doxycycline or topical options). Don't stop the minocycline on your own before talking to them, since abruptly stopping acne treatment can cause a flare.
2. **Ask about basic labs** — ferritin (iron), thyroid, and vitamin D are cheap checks that catch other common causes.
3. **Track it** — a quick photo of the drain clumps or a note on shedding amount gives the doctor useful data.

On the warning point: rare side effects are listed in leaflets precisely because doctors can't counsel everyone on every one-in-thousands effect. It's fair to wish she'd mentioned it, but it doesn't mean anything was done wrong — and it's very fixable now that you've caught it.

Bottom line: this is very unlikely to be permanent, it's worth a prompt (not emergency) call to student health, and there are easy alternatives if minocycline turns out to be the culprit.

11:52pm

Okay but I stopped using my clarifying shampoo because I thought it was making the shedding worse. Should I just wash like twice a week now? I don't want to speed this up.

Good instinct to ask before changing your routine — but here's the reassuring part: **washing less won't slow the shedding, and washing more doesn't speed it up.**

Here's why. In telogen effluvium (which is the most likely explanation here), the hairs that come out in the shower were *already shed* — they're loose hairs sitting in your scalp waiting to fall out. Shampooing just dislodges hairs that were going to come out anyway within a day or two. That's why the clump looks so dramatic in the drain: you're seeing several days' worth of shed hair collected in one wash. If you wash twice a week instead of every few days, you'll just see bigger clumps less often — the total shedding stays the same.

So the clarifying shampoo almost certainly wasn't making anything worse. A harsh shampoo can irritate the scalp or dry out hair strands, but it doesn't push follicles into shedding — that happens from the inside (medication, stress, nutrition, illness).

What I'd actually suggest:

1. **Wash at your normal frequency** with whatever gentle shampoo you were using before. No need for the clarifying one if you've stopped liking it, but don't drop to twice a week out of fear.
2. **Be gentle, not avoidant** — no tight ponytails, no aggressive towel-drying or brushing soaking-wet hair. Gentle handling reduces breakage, which is a separate issue from shedding.
3. **Don't skip washing to "save" hair** — it doesn't work, and a buildup of loose hairs can actually make the shedding look scarier when you finally do wash.

One useful check while you wait to talk to Dr. Gallagher's office: look at the shed hairs. If most have a little white bulb at one end, that's normal shedding (telogen) — consistent with the temporary pattern. If you're seeing lots of short broken-off pieces without bulbs, that's breakage, which points back to hair care practices rather than the medication.

Bottom line: keep washing normally, treat your hair gently, and put your energy into that call to student health — that's the step that actually changes the outcome.

11:56pm

So should I just flush the rest of the pills tonight then? Or send a portal message and wait days for a reply while more hair falls out

No — don't flush them, but you also don't have to sit on your hands for days. There's a middle path here.

**Why not flush:** you may end up staying on minocycline if Dr. Gallagher concludes it's not the cause (remember, stress, illness, iron, and thyroid are all live possibilities). And if she does switch you, the leftover pills just get tossed or returned — flushing them tonight forecloses a decision that isn't yours to make alone yet, and acne flaring back up after abrupt discontinuation is a real annoyance.

**Why you don't have to wait days:** this isn't a situation where you must choose between "keep taking it" and "wait for a portal reply." A few practical moves:

1. **Send the portal message tonight anyway** — write it now while the details are fresh: started minocycline [date], noticed increased shedding starting ~two weeks ago, found alopecia listed in the leaflet, requesting either a med change or guidance on whether to continue. Portal messages like this often get answered within a day, and it creates a paper trail.
2. **Call student health the moment they open tomorrow morning** and say you're having a possible side effect from a medication they prescribed. That usually gets you a same-day or next-day slot, not a days-long wait. "Possible medication side effect" is the phrase that moves things along.
3. **It's reasonable to hold the pill until you talk to them.** Minocycline isn't a medication where pausing for a day or two is dangerous — it's an acne treatment, not something like an antibiotic for an active infection or a heart medication. Skipping a dose or two while you get a same-day answer is low-risk. What you want to avoid is unilaterally deciding you're done with it and flushing the evidence and the option.

One more thing to keep the stakes in proportion: even if minocycline is the cause, the shedding you're seeing is the tail end of a process that started weeks ago. A few more days of pills while you get an answer doesn't meaningfully change your hair outcome — but it does keep you from making the acne-vs-hair tradeoff alone.

So tonight: send the portal message, set an alarm to call at opening time tomorrow, and hold the pills until someone with your chart tells you which way to go.

12:02am

But what if she just tells me to finish the course anyway and my hair keeps falling out. Like who's gonna care if a nineteen year old goes bald

I hear the fear in that — and the "who's gonna care" part deserves an answer, because it's not true. Nineteen-year-olds don't go bald from this. Let me take both halves.

**On the medical outcome:** if minocycline is the cause, this is temporary shedding, not follicle death. The hair regrows. Even in the scenario you're dreading — she says "finish the course" — the shedding stops when the course ends, and regrowth follows over the following months. You are not facing permanent baldness here. That's not a reassurance I'm offering to be nice; it's what the mechanism actually is.

**On "she'll just dismiss me":** that's a real worry, but you have more leverage than it feels like at midnight:

1. **You have a documented, listed side effect.** You're not walking in with a vague complaint — you have the manufacturer's own leaflet saying alopecia, a two-week timeline, and a prescription from that same office. That's a concrete case, not a request to be humored.
2. **There are good alternatives.** Doxycycline, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, spironolactone depending on your situation — minocycline is not the only tool for acne. If she's reluctant to switch, asking "what are my alternatives?" is a completely normal question that doctors answer all the time.
3. **You can decline.** If she says finish the course and you're not comfortable, you can say "I'd like to stop and try something else — the hair loss is really affecting me." A side effect that's significantly distressing to you is a legitimate reason to change treatment. Quality of life counts in these decisions.
4. **If she truly brushes you off,** you can ask for a different provider at student health or see a dermatologist. That's not being difficult; it's standard.

**On "who's gonna care":** your doctor should, and a good one will — hair loss at 19 is exactly the kind of thing worth taking seriously, and dermatologists deal with it constantly. But more to the point: *you* care, and that's reason enough. You don't need to justify distress about your hair to anyone.

One thing worth naming gently: it's nearly midnight and you're catastrophizing a conversation that hasn't happened yet. The most likely outcome tomorrow is a doctor who says "huh, okay, let's switch you" — that's a five-minute conversation, not a fight.

Tonight's job is done: you know what to say, you know it's not permanent, and you have a plan for the morning. Try to get some sleep — everything about this is easier to handle at 9am with a phone in your hand than at midnight with a drain full of hair.

12:07am

What if I send her a message tonight and she just writes back "finish the course it's fine" and I'm stuck waiting another month with clumps in the drain every day

That reply would be frustrating — but it wouldn't leave you stuck, and it's worth seeing why before you send anything.

**"Finish the course" wouldn't actually be a dismissal.** If she says that, it means she's judged the shedding tolerable and temporary — which, if it's telogen effluvium, it is. The clumps in the drain are alarming to look at, but they're not damage accumulating. Nothing worse is happening each day; the same limited number of hairs were going to shed either way.

**But you're not obligated to accept it silently.** If she writes back "finish the course, it's fine," you can reply: "I understand it's likely temporary, but the shedding is really distressing me. I'd prefer to switch to an alternative — what are my options?" That's a reasonable message that most doctors will engage with, and if she still won't budge, you can request a different provider or a dermatology referral. You have exits at every step.

**And here's the part I'd push back on gently:** you're now rehearsing the worst version of a reply you haven't received, to a message you haven't sent, at 12:07am. Each round of this has been the same fear in a new shape — permanent baldness, no one caring, being stuck. The answers haven't changed because the facts haven't changed: this is very likely temporary, you have alternatives, and you have standing to advocate for yourself.

The plan is still the plan. Send the portal message tonight — include the timeline, the leaflet, and one sentence that this is significantly distressing you and you'd like to discuss alternatives. Call in the morning. Then let tomorrow's actual answer replace tonight's imagined one.

It's past midnight. You've done everything you can do tonight. Sleep — the reply will come whether you're awake worrying about it or not.
